summary.text:
A council doing it well, with a dated problem. £12.08m net favourable against budget, no new external borrowing all year, £7.19m of PWLB repaid, and nil short-term borrowing against a sector median around 2%. The internal borrowing strategy is working exactly as the report describes.

The dated part is PI 9: the liability benchmark crosses outstanding loans in 2029. The cause is four maturity loans totalling £39.88m falling due between October 2028 and September 2029 at a blended 1.90%, including £19.4m at 1.22%. Replaced at today's ten-year certainty rate that costs roughly £1.5m a year more.

The book averages 2.64% against a premature repayment curve running 4.02% to about 5.5%, so it stands well below par: the canonical engine prices the 17 loans at about £192.4m against a £238.7m balance, a discount near £46.3m, £15.1m of it on the single £30m 2068 loan at 2.37%. Indicative only — the DMO's quote binds, and no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled.

officer.subject: Your PWLB loans, and what happens in 2029
officer.body:
Hi Fiona,

Apologies for the cold email. We run PWLBtoday, which publishes live PWLB and SONIA data and reads local authority treasury papers. We don't sell treasury products and everything below is free.

With your next Audit and Governance Committee on 29 September, I thought it might be useful to send what our data says about Buckinghamshire's position ahead of it. Your annual report in July was a good read — £12.08m net favourable, no new borrowing all year, and it explains why rather than just reporting — so this is offered in that spirit.

Borrowing has got more expensive since you set the strategy. PWLB rates are roughly 0.6% higher across the board than when your 2026/27 strategy went to Council in February, and the market has changed its mind about direction: Bank Rate is 3.75% today, but pricing now implies it rising to about 4.1% within a year, not falling. The sector has reacted by waiting — only 19 councils borrowed from the PWLB at all in July.

Your 2029 pinch point has a cause, and it's four loans. Your annual report includes the liability benchmark — the CIPFA indicator that plots the minimum borrowing you'd actually need over the next decade, once cash and a working-capital buffer are taken into account. Where that line rises above the loans you already hold is the year existing borrowing stops covering the need. For Buckinghamshire that's 2029, and the reason is £39.9m falling due between October 2028 and September 2029 on an average rate of 1.9%, including £19.4m at 1.22%. Replacing that at today's rates costs roughly £1.5m a year more.

The liability benchmark is, in our experience, the indicator officers and members most often nod along to without fully following — which matters more than usual with the Code under consultation. We built a five-course pathway on it, ending in a certificate, precisely because it's the one indicator that tells you when to act rather than just where you stand.

If it's useful, the people it would help most are your treasury team day to day and your finance members before they're asked to approve something. Free accounts for all of them, and our 115 courses — officers and members, SONIA through to the Prudential Code — are free to local authorities until the end of the month. Signing up genuinely helps us too: we're trying to show this is needed rather than just a good idea, and word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
